questions.title: What makes a JavaScript function a React component?
explanation: A component is used by React as an element type, follows component naming conventions, returns renderable React nodes, and obeys render purity and Hook rules. Calling it as an ordinary function bypasses React's component identity and lifecycle handling.

questions.title: Why must React component names start with a capital letter?
explanation: JSX treats lowercase tags as built-in platform elements such as div, while capitalized tags are resolved as JavaScript component values. Capitalization therefore distinguishes custom components from host elements.

questions.title: How is JSX different from an HTML template?
explanation: JSX is syntax embedded in JavaScript that produces React elements, so expressions, variables, and component composition follow JavaScript rules. It resembles HTML but uses JavaScript property naming and requires a single returned tree.

questions.title: Why does this JSX expression render zero?
explanation: The && operator returns its left operand when that value is falsy. React renders numbers, so a count of zero becomes visible text. Use an explicit comparison such as count > 0 && to return false instead.

questions.title: When should a component return null?
explanation: Returning null is appropriate when the component intentionally renders nothing for the current inputs. If the parent already owns the condition, conditionally including the component there can make the tree and data flow clearer.

questions.title: Why should a list key come from the data rather than be generated during rendering?
explanation: A generated key changes on every render, so React treats each item as new, destroys state and DOM, and recreates the list. Use a stable identifier that represents the same item across renders.

questions.title: What scope must React keys be unique within?
explanation: Keys need to be unique among siblings in the same array or iterator result, not globally across the application. The same stable key may be reused in separate lists.

questions.title: Why is key not available as a normal component prop?
explanation: key is special information consumed by React during reconciliation and is not forwarded to the component. If the component needs the identifier, pass it separately with a domain name such as itemId.

questions.title: What happens when a component's key changes?
explanation: React treats the element as a different component identity, unmounting the old subtree and mounting a new one with fresh state. This is useful for intentional resets but destructive when keys change accidentally.

questions.title: How do props differ from state?
explanation: Props are inputs supplied by a parent for a particular render; state is component-owned memory updated through React. Both are read-only snapshots during rendering, so neither should be mutated directly.

questions.title: Why should a component not mutate an object received through props?
explanation: The object belongs to another component's snapshot and may be shared elsewhere. Mutation creates hidden data flow and React may not know an update occurred; request a parent update or create a new value.

questions.title: What does render purity require from a React component?
explanation: Given the same props, state, and context, rendering should calculate the same JSX without changing pre-existing objects or external systems. Side effects belong in event handlers or synchronization Effects.

questions.title: Why can StrictMode call component functions more than once in development?
explanation: Development Strict Mode intentionally repeats selected render and Effect lifecycles to expose impure rendering and missing cleanup. Production does not perform the extra diagnostic cycle, but code should be correct under it.

questions.title: When is component composition preferable to a large configurable component?
explanation: Composition is preferable when independent pieces, slots, or children express variation clearly. It keeps contracts local and avoids a growing matrix of boolean props that produce invalid combinations.

questions.title: How does event propagation work in React?
explanation: Most React events bubble through the React component tree from the target toward ancestors. A handler can stop propagation when necessary, though explicit handler composition is often easier to trace than relying on distant bubbling.

questions.title: Why must an event handler be passed rather than called during render?
explanation: onClick expects a function. Calling handleSave() executes during rendering and passes its return value as the handler, potentially causing updates or network work on every render.

questions.title: Why does setCount(count + 1) three times usually increment only once?
explanation: All three calls read count from the same render snapshot and enqueue the same replacement value. Functional updaters such as setCount(c => c + 1) are processed in sequence and express dependence on prior queued state.

source.title: Queueing a Series of State Updates

questions.title: When should a functional state updater be used?
explanation: Use it when the next value depends on the previous value, especially for multiple queued updates or callbacks that may run later. If the new value replaces state independently, a direct value remains clear.

questions.title: Why must objects in React state be replaced rather than mutated?
explanation: React treats state as an immutable snapshot and uses identity to detect changed values and enable optimizations. Create a new object containing the updated fields so past renders remain stable and the update is observable.

questions.title: How should a deeply nested state update be simplified?
explanation: First consider flattening or normalizing the state so updates touch fewer levels. When nesting reflects the domain, copy each changed path or use an immutable-update helper while preserving new identities only where values changed.

questions.title: Why is copying an array with spread not enough before mutating an object inside it?
explanation: The new array still contains references to the original item objects, so mutating an item changes prior state. Copy the changed item too, typically with map and object spread.

questions.title: What state structure prevents contradictory UI states?
explanation: Model mutually exclusive modes with one status value or reducer state instead of several booleans that can disagree. Derive booleans such as isLoading from that canonical state and keep only information required for rendering or future updates.

questions.title: Why should duplicated state be removed?
explanation: Two state fields representing the same fact can drift when one update path changes only one copy. Store the minimal source of truth and calculate dependent values during rendering.

questions.title: When should state be colocated rather than moved to a global store?
explanation: Keep state near the smallest subtree that owns and changes it. Colocation limits rerenders, dependencies, and invalid states; lift or externalize only when multiple distant consumers genuinely coordinate around the same source of truth.

questions.title: How does React associate state with a component?
explanation: State is associated with a component's position and identity in the rendered tree, not with the function declaration itself. Changing type, position, or key can reset that state.

questions.title: Why does defining a component inside another component reset its state?
explanation: Each parent render creates a different component function identity, so React sees a new component type and remounts it. Define component types at module scope and pass data through props.

questions.title: What properties should a reducer have?
explanation: A reducer should be pure, avoid mutating existing state, and return the next state from the current state and action. Actions should describe what happened so the transition logic remains centralized and testable.

source.title: Extracting State Logic into a Reducer

questions.title: How can reducer and context be combined without one oversized context?
explanation: Provide state and dispatch through separate contexts or expose domain-specific custom Hooks. Components that only dispatch need not subscribe to every state change, and the reducer retains one audited transition boundary.

source.title: Scaling Up with Reducer and Context

questions.title: Why can an inline object passed to Context cause extra renders?
explanation: A new object identity is created on every provider render, so all consumers observe a changed context value. Split contexts, stabilize values when measured as necessary, and avoid putting frequently changing unrelated data into one context.

questions.title: When should useRef store a value instead of useState?
explanation: Use a ref for mutable information that does not affect rendered output, such as a timer ID or imperative instance. Use state when a change must appear in the UI because ref mutation does not schedule a render.

questions.title: What is an Effect intended to synchronize?
explanation: An Effect synchronizes a component with an external system such as a network connection, browser API, widget, subscription, or non-React state. Pure data transformations for rendering usually do not need an Effect.

questions.title: Why does this Effect create an infinite update loop?
explanation: The Effect updates state, that update causes another render, and without a limiting dependency condition the Effect runs again. Calculate render data directly or identify the actual external synchronization and dependencies.

source.title: My Effect Keeps Re-running in an Infinite Cycle

questions.title: Why should an Effect dependency not be omitted to silence the linter?
explanation: Every reactive value read by the Effect belongs in its dependency list. Omitting one creates a stale closure; instead restructure the code, move non-reactive logic, or prove the value is stable.

questions.title: How does Object.is affect Effect dependency comparison?
explanation: React compares each dependency with its previous value using Object.is. Newly created objects and functions therefore count as changed even when their contents or behavior appear equivalent.

questions.title: How can an object dependency be removed from an Effect?
explanation: Move object construction inside the Effect or depend on the primitive values used to create it. This prevents a new render-time object identity from reconnecting an external system unnecessarily.

questions.title: Why is an async Effect callback invalid as the Effect itself?
explanation: An async function returns a Promise, but React expects the callback to return either nothing or a cleanup function. Define and call an inner async function, and make cleanup prevent stale results or cancel supported work.

questions.title: How can an Effect avoid applying a stale fetch result?
explanation: Cleanup can mark the old request result as ignored or abort the request when the API supports cancellation. Framework data loading or a cache can additionally deduplicate, preload, and avoid client-side waterfalls.

questions.title: When is useLayoutEffect justified?
explanation: useLayoutEffect runs before paint and is appropriate when DOM measurement must synchronously affect the same visual frame. Prefer useEffect for non-visual synchronization because layout Effects block painting and do not run during server rendering.

questions.title: What problem does useEffectEvent solve?
explanation: It extracts non-reactive logic that needs the latest props or state from an Effect. The Effect can then react only to its true synchronization dependencies while the Effect Event reads current values when invoked.

questions.title: Why should an Effect Event not be used to hide a real dependency?
explanation: Effect Events are for logic that should not cause resynchronization. If a value changes which external resource is connected or what the Effect synchronizes, it remains a dependency; hiding it creates stale behavior.

questions.title: When should logic move from an Effect to an event handler?
explanation: If work happens because the user performed a specific action, put it in that event handler. Effects are for consequences of a component being rendered and connected to an external system, not for replaying user intent indirectly from state.

source.title: You Might Not Need an Effect

questions.title: How should a custom Hook be named and structured?
explanation: Its name starts with use and it may call other Hooks at the top level. A custom Hook shares stateful logic, not the same state instance; each call remains independent unless it subscribes to shared external state.

questions.title: What does the Rules of Hooks top-level requirement protect?
explanation: React relies on Hooks being called in the same order on every render. Calling them conditionally, in loops, after early returns, or in ordinary callbacks can shift that order and associate state with the wrong call.

questions.title: How can conditional behavior be expressed without calling a Hook conditionally?
explanation: Call the Hook unconditionally and place the condition inside its callback or parameters, or split the conditional branch into a component that calls its own Hooks. The call order then stays stable.

questions.title: What makes a custom subscription Hook robust?
explanation: It defines subscription and cleanup, exposes a stable snapshot, handles server rendering when applicable, and prevents tearing during concurrent updates. For external mutable stores, useSyncExternalStore provides the required React contract.

questions.title: Why should useId not generate list keys?
explanation: useId creates IDs for accessibility relationships that remain consistent across client and server rendering. List keys must come from stable data identity; calling Hooks per item also breaks when list length changes.

questions.title: How does useImperativeHandle limit a component's exposed ref API?
explanation: It lets a component expose a small imperative handle, such as focus or scroll methods, instead of its entire DOM node. Declarative props remain preferable for behavior that can be expressed through rendering.

questions.title: When is a callback ref useful?
explanation: A callback ref is useful when code must react as a node is attached or detached or maintain a collection of nodes. The callback should return cleanup when supported or handle null/detachment without leaking entries.

questions.title: Why is reading or writing ref.current during render risky?
explanation: Rendering should be repeatable and free of hidden mutation. Ref access during render can make output depend on call history that React cannot track, breaking assumptions used by concurrent rendering and optimization.

questions.title: How should a third-party DOM widget be integrated with React?
explanation: Own a wrapper element with a ref, create and synchronize the widget in an Effect, and destroy subscriptions or instances in cleanup. Define clearly whether React or the widget owns each DOM subtree.

questions.title: What problem does React.memo solve?
explanation: memo can skip rerendering a component when its props compare equal, reducing expensive render work. It is a performance optimization rather than a correctness tool; context and the component's own state can still trigger renders.

questions.title: Why can React.memo be ineffective when a parent passes an inline object?
explanation: The object receives a new identity each render, so shallow prop comparison sees a change. Pass stable primitives, move construction, or memoize the object only after profiling shows that skipped work is valuable.

questions.title: How do useMemo and useCallback differ?
explanation: useMemo caches the result of calling a calculation; useCallback caches the function definition itself. Both depend on accurate dependencies and should address measured identity or computation costs rather than routine correctness.

questions.title: Why must a useMemo calculation remain pure?
explanation: React may call the calculation again, discard its cache, or run it twice in development. Side effects inside it can therefore duplicate work or corrupt external state; useMemo is only a cache for a render calculation.

questions.title: When should a custom memo comparison function be avoided?
explanation: A custom comparator can be slower than rerendering and may capture stale functions if it fails to compare every prop. Profile it with production builds and prefer simpler prop shapes or component boundaries first.

questions.title: What does useDeferredValue defer?
explanation: It lets a non-critical part of the UI lag behind a rapidly changing value while urgent updates such as typing render first. It does not delay the source update or replace network debouncing.

questions.title: How is debouncing different from useDeferredValue?
explanation: Debouncing waits a time interval before starting work and reduces how often work runs. useDeferredValue starts React rendering with lower priority and adapts to device speed; each deferred render may still occur unless interrupted.

questions.title: Why can a transition not control a text input value?
explanation: Controlled text input state must update synchronously so the DOM stays aligned with typing. Update the input urgently and use a transition or deferred value for slower derived content.

questions.title: What does isPending from useTransition represent?
explanation: It indicates that a transition has started and has not completed, allowing the existing UI to remain visible with a pending affordance. It can cover multiple Actions within the transition.

questions.title: How does Suspense coordinate a loading boundary?
explanation: When a supported child suspends, React can show the nearest fallback and later reveal the completed tree. Data fetching must integrate through a Suspense-enabled framework or resource; fetching in an Effect does not automatically activate Suspense.

questions.title: Where should Suspense boundaries be placed?
explanation: Place boundaries around meaningful loading sequences designed with the product experience, not mechanically around every component. Nested boundaries can progressively reveal independent regions while preserving already visible content during transitions.

questions.title: Why can a Suspense fallback flash during navigation?
explanation: An urgent update that suspends may replace visible content with the nearest fallback. Mark navigation as a transition so React can keep revealed content visible while the next screen prepares, with an explicit pending indicator.

source.title: Preventing Already Revealed Content from Hiding

questions.title: How does lazy load a component?
explanation: lazy defers calling a module loader until React first attempts to render the component, caches the Promise and resolved default export, and suspends while loading. Render it under Suspense and handle rejected imports with an error boundary.

questions.title: What performance information should be collected before adding memoization?
explanation: Use React DevTools Profiler and browser performance tools to identify slow commits, frequently rerendered subtrees, and expensive calculations in a production build. Optimize the measured bottleneck and verify the improvement against complexity and memory cost.

questions.title: How can a large list be rendered efficiently?
explanation: Keep stable keys and item props, avoid repeated expensive work, and virtualize when only a window is visible. Windowing makes render and DOM cost proportional to visible rows plus overscan rather than the entire collection, while focus and accessibility behavior need deliberate handling.

questions.title: What makes an input controlled in React?
explanation: Passing value or checked makes React state the source of truth, and an onChange handler must synchronously update that value. defaultValue or defaultChecked initializes an uncontrolled input whose current value remains in the DOM.

questions.title: Why does a controlled input become read-only?
explanation: If value is supplied without an onChange that updates it, every render forces the same value back into the DOM. Add a synchronous state update, use readOnly intentionally, or use defaultValue for uncontrolled behavior.

questions.title: Why should an input not switch between controlled and uncontrolled?
explanation: The ownership model would change during the component lifetime and can lose or overwrite DOM state. Initialize controlled values to an appropriate non-null value and keep the mode stable.

questions.title: What happens when a function is passed to a form action prop?
explanation: React treats it as an Action and calls it with FormData when the form submits. Uncontrolled fields reset after successful completion, and related form Hooks can expose action state and pending status.

questions.title: What does useActionState manage?
explanation: It connects an Action with state derived from its result and exposes a dispatching action plus pending status. The action receives prior state before its normal arguments, which is important when adapting an existing function.

questions.title: Why might a useActionState action read the wrong FormData argument?
explanation: The wrapped action's first argument is the previous state, so FormData becomes the second argument. Forgetting the inserted parameter makes code interpret state as submission data.

questions.title: What can useFormStatus read?
explanation: A component rendered inside a form can read the parent form's pending state, submitted data, method, and action. The Hook does not observe a form rendered by the same component above its call; place the status component as a child.

questions.title: When should useOptimistic be used?
explanation: Use it when immediate temporary feedback improves an Action-driven experience and the optimistic result can be reconciled with the authoritative outcome. Clearly represent pending state and restore or explain failure rather than silently leaving false data.

questions.title: How should an optimistic list item receive identity?
explanation: Give the temporary item a stable client-generated identity separate from its eventual server identifier, then reconcile on success. Avoid array-index keys so insertion, failure, and replacement preserve the correct item state.

questions.title: Why should form validation still run on the server?
explanation: Client validation improves feedback but can be bypassed and may run against stale rules. The server remains authoritative for validation, authorization, and invariants, returning safe field or form errors that the React UI can display.

questions.title: How should accessible validation errors be connected to inputs?
explanation: Render a clear message with a stable ID, associate it using aria-describedby or the platform's applicable attributes, mark invalid state, move focus or provide a summary when appropriate, and do not rely on color alone.

questions.title: Why is dangerouslySetInnerHTML dangerous?
explanation: It inserts raw HTML and bypasses React's normal text escaping, so untrusted content can create cross-site scripting. Sanitize with a well-maintained policy at a trusted boundary and avoid mixing managed children with that element.

questions.title: How should a reusable button preserve native semantics?
explanation: Render a real button for button behavior, forward relevant props and refs, preserve keyboard and focus behavior, and default type intentionally inside forms. A styled div with click handling requires rebuilding semantics and remains error-prone.

questions.title: What does useId solve for accessibility?
explanation: It creates stable IDs that can connect labels, descriptions, hints, and inputs and remain consistent through server rendering and hydration. It is not for database identity or list keys.

questions.title: How can a form offer several submission actions?
explanation: Buttons can supply distinct formAction functions, allowing operations such as save draft and publish within one form. Each action must enforce its own server-side validation and authorization rather than trusting the clicked label.

questions.title: When should createPortal be used?
explanation: Use a portal when content such as a modal or tooltip must escape DOM clipping or stacking containers while remaining a child in the React tree. Context and React event bubbling follow the React tree, not the physical DOM placement.

questions.title: Why can a click inside a portal trigger a parent React handler?
explanation: Portal events propagate according to the React component tree even though the DOM node is elsewhere. Stop propagation when appropriate or place the portal higher in the React tree if that better matches ownership.

questions.title: When is flushSync justified?
explanation: It is a last resort for integrations that require the DOM to reflect an update synchronously before the next line, such as certain browser callbacks. It can hurt performance and reveal Suspense fallbacks, so normal React scheduling is preferable.

questions.title: What is the difference between createRoot and hydrateRoot?
explanation: createRoot takes ownership of a client-rendered container and normally replaces its contents on first render. hydrateRoot attaches React behavior to HTML already produced by compatible server rendering and expects matching output.

questions.title: Why is suppressHydrationWarning only an escape hatch?
explanation: It silences a known one-level text or attribute mismatch and React may not patch that content. It does not solve divergent trees; deterministic rendering or a deliberate client-only second pass should address the root cause.

questions.title: How can locale-sensitive rendering cause hydration mismatches?
explanation: Server and browser locale, timezone, or runtime data can format different text for the first render. Pass the same locale and serialized value, preformat consistently, or defer browser-specific output until after hydration.

questions.title: Why should recoverable hydration errors be reported?
explanation: A root error callback can send recoverable errors and component stacks to observability, revealing mismatches that otherwise remain development warnings or subtle production defects. Reports should be sampled and scrubbed of sensitive data.

questions.title: How does streaming server rendering improve initial delivery?
explanation: Streaming APIs can send an HTML shell and completed Suspense regions progressively instead of waiting for the entire tree. The server must handle aborts, errors, status decisions, and safe insertion into a complete document.

questions.title: Why is renderToString limited for Suspense data?
explanation: renderToString cannot wait for suspended data or progressively stream boundaries; it sends the fallback immediately. Use a streaming server API or framework integration when Suspense-aware SSR is required.

questions.title: How should multiple React roots avoid useId collisions?
explanation: Pass a distinct identifierPrefix when creating or hydrating each root, and use the same prefix on server and client for that root. This keeps generated accessibility IDs unique and hydration-compatible.

questions.title: How do Server Components differ from SSR?
explanation: Server Components execute in a separate server/build environment and their component code is not sent to the client, while SSR produces initial HTML for a client component tree that later hydrates. Frameworks can combine both techniques.

questions.title: What does the 'use client' directive define?
explanation: It marks a module boundary whose exports are client components and can use client-only features such as state and browser events. Modules imported beneath that boundary join the client bundle, so place it narrowly.

questions.title: What values may cross from a Server Component to a Client Component?
explanation: Props crossing the boundary must be serializable by the React Server Component protocol. Ordinary functions and server-only objects cannot cross, except supported Server Function references and defined serializable types.

questions.title: What security rule applies to every Server Function?
explanation: Treat it as a remotely callable server endpoint: authenticate, authorize the exact resource and action, validate inputs, protect secrets, and return safe errors. UI visibility and captured identifiers are not authorization.

questions.title: What does the 'use server' directive do?
explanation: It marks async server-side functions that compatible frameworks can expose for calls from client code. It does not make a function trusted automatically; framework transport and application security still apply.

questions.title: Why should Server Component framework versions be pinned carefully?
explanation: The user-facing Server Component model is stable in React 19, but bundler and framework implementation APIs may not follow semver between minor versions. Framework authors and infrastructure should use supported, tested version combinations.

questions.title: What does the use API do with a Promise?
explanation: use reads a Promise during rendering: it suspends while pending, returns the fulfilled value, or throws the rejection to the nearest error boundary. Unlike ordinary Hooks, use can appear in loops and conditions, but still only inside a component or Hook.

questions.title: Why should a Promise passed from a Server Component be cached or stable?
explanation: Creating a new Promise during every client render can repeatedly suspend and restart work. Framework-managed or server-created Promises are stable across the relevant render and integrate with request caching.

questions.title: How should a React feature be tested without coupling to implementation details?
explanation: Exercise behavior through rendered output, accessible roles, labels, and user interactions, then assert what a user or external boundary observes. Avoid assertions about private state, Hook order, or component instances that make refactoring fail tests without changing behavior.

questions.title: What production evidence should guide a React performance optimization?
explanation: Measure user-centric latency, bundle and resource waterfalls, React render and commit timings, long tasks, memory, and device/network segments in production-like builds. Fix architecture and unnecessary synchronization first, then verify each memoization, transition, lazy boundary, or virtualization change against the measured bottleneck.
